title: Swift Route Logistics: factoring receivables vs. a short-term bank loan
participant_role: Treasury analyst at Swift Route Logistics comparing two ways to raise cash quickly
judge_role: Chief executive officer (CEO) of Swift Route Logistics, who wants the cheapest financing but is worried about the debt-to-equity ratio

difficulty.rationale: Factoring vs short-term loan cost and leverage trade-off.

scenario:
You are to assume the role of treasury analyst for SWIFT ROUTE LOGISTICS, a regional delivery and freight company. The chief executive officer (CEO) (judge) has asked you to recommend how to solve an immediate cash shortage.

Swift Route Logistics is profitable but short on cash. It has $200,000 of accounts receivable from major retail clients who reliably pay on 60-day terms. The company needs $190,000 in cash this week to fund an emergency expansion of its delivery fleet.

You have researched two ways to get the cash. Option A: sell (factor) all $200,000 of the receivables, without recourse, to a finance company (a factor) that charges a flat 4% fee and deposits the rest of the cash immediately. Option B: borrow $200,000 from the bank for 60 days at a 9% annual interest rate, repaying principal and interest in 60 days when the receivables are collected. The bank uses a 360-day year to compute interest.

[Financing options: see exhibits]

The CEO (judge) wants to keep financing costs low but is also worried about the company's debt-to-equity ratio, which is already close to the maximum allowed by its current lenders.

You must:
- Explain the difference between factoring accounts receivable and taking out a bank loan
- Calculate the total dollar cost of Option A
- Calculate the total dollar cost of Option B for the 60-day period
- Prepare the journal entry to record Option A
- Recommend the better option, balancing cost against the CEO's concern about the debt-to-equity ratio

You will present the information to the CEO (judge) in a role-play to take place in the CEO's (judge's) office. The CEO (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented the information and have answered the CEO's (judge's) questions, the CEO (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.

judge_questions: If one of our retail clients goes bankrupt after we factor the receivables, who takes the loss?
The factor says it could lower its fee if we sell the receivables with recourse. What would that mean for us?

solution.overview: A strong answer computes a factoring fee of $8,000 versus $3,000 of loan interest, and shows that the fee equals about 25% a year compared with the loan's 9%. The presenter then explains that factoring without recourse is a sale of an asset that adds no debt, while the loan adds a $200,000 liability and raises the debt-to-equity ratio, and recommends factoring to protect the lender limit.

answer: Factoring sells the receivables: receivables become cash right away, minus a fee
Without recourse, the factor takes the risk that customers do not pay
A bank loan keeps the receivables and adds a liability (notes payable) that must be repaid with interest
Factoring adds no debt; the loan does
Cash received: 200,000 minus 8,000 = $192,000, enough for the $190,000 need
Annualized: 8,000 / 192,000 = about 4.2% for 60 days, x 6 periods = about 25% a year
Interest = principal x rate x time
Option B is $5,000 cheaper in dollars
Debit Cash $192,000
Debit Loss on Sale of Receivables (factoring fee) $8,000
Credit Accounts Receivable $200,000
The loan is cheaper (9% vs. about 25% a year), but it adds $200,000 of liabilities
More debt with the same equity raises debt-to-equity and could break the lenders' limit
Factoring turns one asset into another, so liabilities and the ratio do not rise
Recommend Option A: the extra $5,000 is the price of protecting our lender agreements; use loans once the ratio improves

judge_question_answers.question: If one of our retail clients goes bankrupt after we factor the receivables, who takes the loss?
answer: Without recourse, the factor takes the loss; Swift Route does not repay the factor
That transfer of credit risk is part of why the fee is 4%
Our receivables are with reliable clients, so we are paying for protection we may not need much

judge_question_answers.question: The factor says it could lower its fee if we sell the receivables with recourse. What would that mean for us?
answer: With recourse, we must pay the factor back for any customer who does not pay, so we keep the credit risk
We would record a recourse liability for expected losses, or, if we keep control of the receivables, the deal is treated as a secured borrowing
A borrowing adds debt and could raise the debt-to-equity ratio, which defeats the purpose
A lower fee may still be worth it only if the deal qualifies as a sale and our clients are very reliable

key_concepts.definition: Selling accounts receivable to a finance company (factor) for immediate cash, minus a fee.
The factor bears the loss if customers do not pay; the seller has no obligation to repay.
The seller must repay the factor for receivables that are not collected, so it keeps the credit risk.
The expense recorded for the factoring fee. Fee = receivables sold x fee rate.
Interest = principal x annual rate x time (days / 360 for a banker's year).
A short-term cost converted to a yearly rate so options can be compared. Annual rate = (cost / cash received) x (360 / days).
Total liabilities / total equity. A higher ratio means more borrowing relative to owners' investment.
A condition in a loan agreement, such as a maximum debt-to-equity ratio, that the borrower must meet.
Amounts customers owe the business for goods or services sold on credit. A current asset on the balance sheet.
A written promise to repay borrowed money with interest; a liability on the balance sheet.

items.label: Explain the nature of accounts receivable

criteria.exceeds: Explains that factoring sells the $200,000 of receivables for immediate cash minus a fee, that without recourse the factor takes the risk that customers do not pay, and that a bank loan keeps the receivables and adds a notes payable liability that must be repaid with interest.
criteria.meets: Explains that factoring is a sale of receivables that adds no debt, while the bank loan keeps the receivables and adds a liability.
criteria.below: Describes factoring and the loan vaguely, or does not explain what without recourse means.
criteria.little: Does not explain the difference between factoring and a bank loan, or describes factoring as a type of loan.

criteria.exceeds: Calculates the $8,000 factoring fee ($200,000 x 4%) and $192,000 of cash received, confirms it covers the $190,000 need, and converts the fee to an annual rate of about 25% (8,000 / 192,000 = about 4.2% per 60 days, x 6).
criteria.meets: Calculates the $8,000 factoring fee and the $192,000 of cash received.
criteria.below: Gets the fee right but not the cash received, or does not check that the cash covers the $190,000 need.
criteria.little: Does not calculate the cost of factoring, or the numbers are unrelated to the exhibit.

criteria.exceeds: Calculates loan interest of $3,000 ($200,000 x 9% x 60/360), shows the loan is $5,000 cheaper in dollars, and compares annual rates (about 25% for factoring vs. 9% for the loan) to explain what the extra cost buys.
criteria.meets: Calculates $3,000 of interest using a 360-day year and states that the loan is $5,000 cheaper than factoring.
criteria.below: Uses the wrong time period (such as a full year of $18,000 interest or a 365-day year) or does not compare the two costs.
criteria.little: Does not calculate the cost of the loan.

criteria.exceeds: Records debit Cash $192,000, debit Loss on Sale of Receivables (factoring fee) $8,000, credit Accounts Receivable $200,000, and contrasts it with the loan entry (debit Cash $200,000, credit Notes Payable $200,000).
criteria.meets: Records debit Cash $192,000, debit Loss on Sale of Receivables $8,000 and credit Accounts Receivable $200,000.
criteria.below: Uses the right accounts with wrong amounts, leaves out the fee, or credits a liability instead of Accounts Receivable.
criteria.little: Gives no journal entry, or an entry with unrelated accounts.

items.label: Explain the nature of balance sheets

criteria.exceeds: Explains debt-to-equity as total liabilities divided by total equity, shows that factoring turns one asset into another so liabilities and the ratio do not rise, while the loan adds $200,000 of liabilities and could break the lenders' limit, and recommends Option A as the price of protecting the lender agreements.
criteria.meets: Explains that the loan adds $200,000 of liabilities and raises debt-to-equity while factoring does not, and recommends factoring.
criteria.below: Recommends an option based only on dollar cost, or mentions the ratio without explaining how each option affects liabilities.
criteria.little: Does not address the balance sheet or the debt-to-equity concern.

items.label: Critical Thinking: Reason effectively and use systems thinking

criteria.exceeds: Weighs the $5,000 extra cost against the risk of breaking the lender limit and connects each option to the balance sheet and the ratio.
criteria.meets: Reasons correctly from the exhibit to the costs of both options and their effect on debt.
criteria.below: Reaches a conclusion without showing the reasoning, or looks only at dollar cost.

items.label: Problem Solving: Make judgments and decisions and solve problems

criteria.exceeds: Recommends factoring now to protect the lender agreements and suggests using bank loans once the ratio improves.
criteria.meets: Makes a clear recommendation of Option A that balances cost against the debt-to-equity concern.
criteria.below: Hesitates, or recommends the loan without addressing the lender limit.

criteria.exceeds: Explains factoring, interest and debt-to-equity in plain language the CEO can follow, in a logical order, with confident and professional delivery.
criteria.meets: Presents the costs, entry and recommendation clearly and in an organized way.
criteria.below: Presentation is hard to follow, relies on jargon, or skips steps.

items.label: Creativity and Innovation: Show evidence of creativity

criteria.exceeds: Uses a side by side comparison of the two options (cost, cash received, annual rate, effect on liabilities) that makes the tradeoff obvious.
criteria.meets: Organizes the information in a way that makes the two options easy to compare.
criteria.below: Presents the facts with little effort to make them engaging or easy to follow.
criteria.little: Shows no evidence of creativity or original thought.

items.label: Overall impression and responses to the judge's questions

criteria.exceeds: Answers both questions correctly and confidently: without recourse the factor takes the bankruptcy loss, which is part of why the fee is 4%; and with recourse Swift Route keeps the credit risk, must record a recourse liability or treat the deal as a secured borrowing, which could add debt and raise the ratio.
criteria.meets: Answers both questions mostly correctly, including that the factor bears the loss and that recourse keeps the risk with Swift Route.
criteria.below: Answers only one question correctly, or gives vague answers.
criteria.little: Cannot answer the judge's questions, or says Swift Route bears the loss on receivables sold without recourse.

key_points: Factoring without recourse sells the receivables and transfers the credit risk; a bank loan keeps the receivables and adds a liability
Option A fee: $200,000 x 4% = $8,000; cash received $192,000, enough for the $190,000 need
Option B interest: $200,000 x 9% x 60/360 = $3,000, so the loan is $5,000 cheaper in dollars
Factoring costs about 25% a year (8,000 / 192,000 = about 4.2% per 60 days, x 6) versus 9% for the loan
Entry: debit Cash $192,000, debit Loss on Sale of Receivables $8,000, credit Accounts Receivable $200,000
The loan adds $200,000 of liabilities and raises debt-to-equity; factoring leaves liabilities unchanged
Recommend Option A to protect the lender limit; the extra $5,000 is the price of that protection
